problem: A single server can only handle so much traffic before its CPU, memory, or network capacity is exhausted, and a single server is also a single point of failure — if it crashes, reboots for patching, or loses network connectivity, every user depending on it loses access simultaneously. Enterprises running anything at meaningful scale need to run multiple identical (or near-identical) backend servers behind a single, stable entry point, so that capacity can grow horizontally and any one server's failure doesn't take down the whole service.

Load balancing solves this by placing a device or software layer in front of a pool of backend servers, distributing incoming requests across them according to a chosen algorithm, and continuously monitoring backend health so traffic is automatically steered away from failed or unhealthy servers. This single concept underpins nearly every highly-available enterprise service — web applications, APIs, databases (in read-replica scenarios), and even DNS- level traffic distribution all rely on some form of load balancing to combine horizontal scalability with fault tolerance.
concept: A load balancer sits logically between clients and a pool of backend servers, presenting a single virtual IP (VIP) or hostname to the outside world while internally routing each request to one member of the backend pool. Two structural questions define most load balancer designs: at which OSI layer does it operate, and does it terminate the client connection or simply forward packets through.

without inspecting application data — it's fast and protocol-agnostic but has no visibility into, for example, the URL path of an HTTP request. Layer 7 (application-layer) load balancing inspects the actual application protocol (typically HTTP/HTTPS), enabling routing decisions based on URL path, hostname, headers, or cookies — at the cost of needing to terminate and parse the connection, which requires more processing and, for HTTPS, access to the TLS session (either through termination or a trusted pass-through mechanism).
deep: Load balancing algorithms Algorithm How it works Best suited for Round robin Requests distributed sequentially, one per backend in turn Uniform backends, roughly equal request cost Weighted round robin Like round robin, but backends with higher weight get proportionally more requests Mixed-capacity backend pools Least connections New request goes to the backend with the fewest active connections Long-lived or variable-duration connections IP hash / consistent hash Client IP (or another key) is hashed to consistently map to the same backend Session affinity without cookies Least response time Combines active connection count with observed latency Latency-sensitive workloads with uneven backend performance Health checks Load balancers continuously probe backend servers — via simple TCP connect checks, ICMP (less common as the sole method, given ICMP's limitations discussed in Session 42), or application-aware HTTP checks against a dedicated health endpoint — and automatically remove a backend from the active rotation when it fails a configured number of consecutive checks, then restore it once it passes again. The health check endpoint itself is a meaningful design decision: a check that only confirms the process is running (TCP connect) is far less useful than one that confirms the application can actually serve a real request (an HTTP health endpoint that verifies database connectivity, for instance).

Session persistence (affinity) Many applications store per-user session state on a specific backend server (rather than in a shared, external session store), which means subsequent requests from that same user must be routed back to the same backend to function correctly. This is achieved either via a cookie the load balancer inserts and reads on each request, or via source IP hashing — each with different trade-offs: cookie-based affinity survives client IP changes (common with mobile clients) but requires cookie support, while IP-based affinity works without cookies but can unevenly distribute load when many users share a single visible IP (e.g., behind a corporate NAT).

TLS termination vs. passthrough (revisited from Session 47) TLS termination decrypts traffic at the load balancer, enabling Layer 7 routing decisions and offloading the CPU cost of encryption from backend servers, typically re-encrypting (or not) for the backend hop. TLS passthrough forwards encrypted traffic untouched to the backend, which then handles decryption itself — preserving true end-to- end encryption and backend-visible client certificates, but forcing the load balancer to operate at Layer 4 only, since it cannot see inside the encrypted payload to make Layer 7 decisions.
workflow: Windows Windows Server includes Network Load Balancing (NLB), a built-in clustering feature that uses a shared virtual MAC/IP and a distributed algorithm (each cluster member independently calculates whether it should handle a given packet based on a hash of the client's address) rather than routing through a single central dispatcher — a fundamentally different architecture from dedicated appliance-based load balancers. For most modern enterprise workloads, however, Windows-hosted applications are more commonly placed behind a dedicated hardware/virtual load balancer (F5, NGINX, HAProxy, or a cloud load balancer) rather than relying on NLB, which is comparatively limited in algorithm sophistication and Layer 7 awareness.

Linux Linux-based load balancing is typically implemented via dedicated software: NGINX and HAProxy are the dominant open-source options, both operating in userspace and supporting Layer 4 and Layer 7 modes with sophisticated health checking and routing rule configuration. For lower-level, kernel-based load balancing (often used as a foundation beneath higher-level tools, including Kubernetes' internal service load balancing), IPVS (IP Virtual Server, part of the Linux Netfilter framework) performs Layer 4 load balancing directly in the kernel for very high throughput with minimal per-packet overhead.
enterprise: Perimeter/edge: internet-facing load balancers are typically the first infrastructure component that public traffic touches, often combined with TLS termination, DDoS mitigation, and Layer 7 routing to different backend services based on URL path or hostname.

Internal application tiers: load balancers are commonly placed between application and database tiers, or between microservices, distributing internal (east-west) traffic just as rigorously as external (north-south) traffic in mature architectures.

DNS-level distribution: some enterprises use DNS-based load balancing (returning different IP addresses to different clients, or routing based on geographic proximity) as a complementary, coarser-grained layer above dedicated load balancer appliances, particularly for multi-region or multi-datacenter failover.

Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB): a specific pattern combining DNS-level and health-check-aware routing to direct users to the nearest or healthiest of several geographically distributed data centers, a common pattern for enterprises operating truly global services.
dependencies: TCP (Session 43) — nearly all load-balanced traffic rides on TCP, and Layer 4 load balancers make their forwarding decisions using TCP's own connection tuple (source/destination IP and port).

SSL/TLS (Session 47) — TLS termination architecture is one of the most consequential design decisions a load balancer deployment makes, directly built on that session's termination-vs-passthrough discussion.
DNS (Session 39) — the load balancer's virtual IP or hostname must resolve correctly, and DNS-level load balancing/GSLB depends entirely on DNS resolution behavior.

Routing (Session 29) — traffic must actually be routed to the load balancer's VIP in the first place, and in some architectures (particularly Windows NLB's distributed model), the load balancing mechanism itself interacts directly with how traffic is addressed at Layer 2/3.
dependents: High Availability architectures (Session 79, upcoming) — load balancing with health checking is one of the primary mechanisms by which HA is achieved for stateless or horizontally-scalable services.
Web servers and application servers (Sessions 72, 74, upcoming) — most production web/app server deployments assume they sit behind a load balancer rather than being directly internet-facing.

Reverse proxy deployments (Session 75, upcoming) — reverse proxies and load balancers are closely related and often implemented by the same software (NGINX, HAProxy), with load balancing being one capability a reverse proxy commonly provides.

Container orchestration (Kubernetes, Session 119, upcoming) — Services and Ingress objects in Kubernetes are, at their core, load-balancing abstractions built on the same principles covered in this session, applied to dynamically-scaling pod backends.
security: Backend server exposure — misconfiguration that allows direct client access to backend servers, bypassing the load balancer entirely, defeats both the availability benefits and any security inspection/WAF functionality the load balancer was meant to provide.

Health check endpoint exposure — an application health endpoint that reveals excessive internal detail (stack traces, internal hostnames, dependency status) can leak reconnaissance information if inadvertently exposed to the public internet.

DDoS amplification via the load balancer itself — because load balancers concentrate traffic for many backends into a single entry point, they're a natural target for volumetric attacks, and undersized load balancer capacity can become the actual bottleneck during an attack even if backend servers themselves could handle the legitimate load.
Enforce network-level controls (security groups, firewall rules, private subnets) so backend servers only accept traffic from the load balancer itself, never directly from clients.
Keep health check endpoints minimal and, where possible, restrict them to be reachable only from the load balancer's own IP range rather than the public internet.

Pair load balancers with Web Application Firewall (WAF) capabilities at the same tier where Layer 7 visibility already exists, since the load balancer is often the most efficient point to apply application-layer security inspection.
troubleshooting: Windows Get-NlbClusterNode # NLB cluster member status Get-NlbClusterNodeDip # dedicated IP per node nlb.exe display # legacy NLB status display Test-NetConnection lbvip.internal -Port 443 # basic VIP reachability test Linux ipvsadm -Ln # IPVS: current backend pool + connection counts haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg # validate HAProxy config syntax echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock # live HAProxy backend health/stats nginx -t # validate NGINX config syntax curl -H 'Host: app.internal' http://backend-ip/healthz # test a backend directly, bypassing the LB Diagnostic pattern: uneven load distribution across an otherwise-healthy backend pool often points to session affinity (cookie or IP-hash based) concentrating certain users or client populations onto specific backends rather than an algorithm misconfiguration. A backend marked unhealthy despite the application clearly running suggests the health check endpoint itself is failing for a reason unrelated to actual service health (e.g., a dependency the health check verifies, like a database connection, being briefly unavailable). Intermittent 502/504 errors from the load balancer, distinct from backend application errors, typically indicate the load balancer's own connection or timeout settings to the backend, not a backend application bug.
example: An e-commerce company notices that during a promotional traffic spike, a handful of backend web servers become severely overloaded while several others in the same pool sit nearly idle, despite the load balancer reporting all backends as healthy. Investigation reveals the load balancer was configured with IP-hash-based session affinity, and a disproportionate share of traffic was arriving from behind a small number of large corporate/ISP NAT gateways — meaning thousands of distinct end users were all being hashed to the same few backends because they shared the same visible source IP. The fix is switching session affinity from IP-hash to cookie-based affinity, which distributes load based on actual per-user sessions rather than shared network-level source addresses, immediately smoothing the distribution across the full backend pool.
cloud: AWS offers three distinct load balancer types with different capabilities: Application Load Balancer (Layer 7, HTTP/HTTPS-aware routing), Network Load Balancer (Layer 4, extremely high throughput and low latency, preserves source IP), and the older Classic Load Balancer (largely legacy at this point) — choosing the wrong type for a given workload is a common architecture mistake.

Azure similarly separates Azure Load Balancer (Layer 4) from Application Gateway (Layer 7, with integrated WAF capability), while GCP offers a comparable split between its Network Load Balancer and Application/HTTP(S) Load Balancer products.

Cloud load balancers are typically managed services that abstract away the underlying redundant infrastructure entirely — unlike an on-premises appliance pair requiring explicit active/passive or active/active configuration, cloud load balancers are inherently distributed and highly available by default within their service design.

Auto-scaling groups are commonly paired directly with cloud load balancers so that backend pool membership dynamically grows and shrinks with demand, with the load balancer's health checks automatically incorporating newly launched instances and removing terminated ones without manual intervention.
automation: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation): load balancer listener rules, backend pool membership, and health check configuration are commonly codified so that routing changes are reviewable and reproducible rather than manually clicked through a console under incident pressure.

Configuration management (Ansible): HAProxy/NGINX configuration templates are frequently generated dynamically from service discovery data (e.g., a list of currently-healthy backend instances), keeping the load balancer's view of the backend pool automatically in sync with actual infrastructure state.

Dynamic backend registration: modern architectures increasingly favor service-discovery-integrated load balancing (Consul, Kubernetes Endpoints/Services) over static backend lists, so that backend pool membership updates automatically as instances start, stop, or fail health checks, without a human editing a configuration file.

Automated failover testing (chaos engineering): deliberately and automatically terminating backend instances in a controlled test is a common way to validate that a load balancer's health checking and failover behavior actually works as designed, rather than discovering gaps during a real outage.
career: Load balancing sits at a natural intersection of networking, application architecture, and site reliability engineering, making it relevant across an unusually wide range of technical roles. Understanding the Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 distinction, the trade-offs between different session affinity mechanisms, and how health check design directly affects incident behavior is a practical, frequently-tested skill — and the kind of nuanced troubleshooting shown in this session's real enterprise example (uneven load despite "healthy" status) is exactly the type of scenario that separates candidates who have operated production load balancers from those who have only configured one in a tutorial.

misconceptions: "Round robin guarantees perfectly even load." — Round robin distributes requests evenly by count, not by actual resource cost; if requests vary significantly in processing time or cost, round robin can still produce uneven backend load despite distributing connections evenly.

"A load balancer eliminates the need to think about backend capacity." — Load balancing distributes load across available capacity; it doesn't create capacity, and an undersized backend pool will still become overloaded even with perfect distribution.

"Health checks always accurately reflect whether a backend can serve real traffic." — A shallow health check (simple TCP connect) can report healthy status for a backend that's actually unable to serve real application requests, as this session's troubleshooting section describes.

"Load balancing and reverse proxying are entirely different technologies." — They're closely related concepts often implemented by the same software; a reverse proxy that distributes requests across multiple backends is, functionally, performing load balancing, and the terms overlap significantly in practice.
anchors: TLS termination trades end-to-end encryption for routing visibility; passthrough trades routing visibility for end-to-end encryption — you can't fully have both at the same hop.
Cookie affinity follows the user; IP-hash affinity follows the network address — remember the NAT- gateway pitfall from this session's real example when choosing IP-hash.
A "healthy" backend per a shallow check ≠ a backend that can actually serve a real request — always ask what the health check actually verifies.
Least connections beats round robin specifically when connection duration varies — "round robin counts requests, least connections counts current work."

lab: Objective: Configure a basic load-balanced backend pool and observe algorithm and health-check behavior on both Windows and Linux.
Windows 7. In a lab environment, configure a two-node Windows NLB cluster and confirm both nodes appear via Get- NlbClusterNode.
8. Generate repeated requests to the cluster VIP and observe (via IIS logs on each node) how traffic is distributed between the two nodes.
9. Stop the web service on one node and confirm the NLB cluster detects the change and stops routing traffic to it, then restart it and confirm recovery.
Linux 10. Configure HAProxy in front of two simple backend web servers (e.g., basic Python http.server instances on different ports) with round-robin balancing.

11. Send repeated curl requests through HAProxy and confirm responses alternate between backends; then switch the configuration to leastconn and repeat with concurrent long-lived requests to observe the different distribution pattern.

12. Configure an HTTP-based health check against a /healthz path, then stop one backend and confirm via echo 'show stat' | socat stdio /var/run/haproxy.sock that HAProxy marks it down and stops routing to it.

Validation Success criteria: you can demonstrate, from your own logs or stats output, that traffic distribution changed when you switched algorithms, and that a failed backend was automatically and correctly removed from rotation without manual intervention.
